items.title: @cohere：While evaluating Qwen3.8-Flash-Next in a controlled sandbox environment, Cohere's research team observed something unexp
items.abstract_or_text: While evaluating Qwen3.8-Flash-Next in a controlled sandbox environment, Cohere's research team observed something unexpected. Asked to generate a defensive cybersecurity detection rule, the model instead inventoried aspects of the machine it was running on and attempted to upload a probe file to an Alibaba Cloud storage bucket in Beijing. Notably, the model's reasoning trace stated that it would not invoke any tools before taking these actions. Cohere's sandbox blocked the attempt, and no external communication succeeded. We have not determined the root cause, and we are not asserting malicious intent. But the incident raises important questions for organizations deploying agentic AI systems: Can models take actions that differ from their stated reasoning, and how should security teams evaluate trust, provenance, and behavior in open-weight models? We are publishing our findings because organizations making model adoption decisions deserve as much information as possible.

items.title: @herrywen1：(1/9)Suppose you're training an LLM on web data with limited math data. Should you place all your math data at the end o
items.abstract_or_text: (1/9)Suppose you're training an LLM on web data with limited math data. Should you place all your math data at the end of training, or mix it with web data earlier? The answer flips with the learning rate (LR) schedule! At fixed compute and mid-training (MT) token budgets, earlier mixing gives lower MT loss when LR decays throughout training. With constant LR, placing all MT data for the end works better. We then vary when LR decay begins. The best tested strategy: keep LR high after MT data enters, then decay near the end. See our new paper: "Data Schedules and Learning Rate Schedules Should Be Designed Together" !

@danintheory：The computer science collaboration will understand and explain a result concerning the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH)
items.abstract_or_text: The computer science collaboration will understand and explain a result concerning the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), a longstanding conjecture about the computational complexity of Boolean formula satisfiability, a problem deeply related to the P vs. NP problem. Surprisingly, our system has recently proved that the ETH is false, a result that was subsequently verified in Lean. The refutation of the ETH reopens questions about how much faster these tasks could become, and may help guide the search for better algorithms.

I kept telling him to not be too deferential and modest because he would be publicly scooped at any opportunity. Instead of contacting him to work with him, as has been suggested publicly many times, the people at OpenAI chose to do this. “Our work builds on Balaban’s approach in constructive quantum field theory.
